_comment: Shared cross-language corpus for the release_external_links gates (PSY-1996).
THE CONTRACT: anything the Go write gate stores must be renderable by the
frontend read gate. Nothing may be storable and unrenderable, or a curator's
save silently produces no link and nobody can see why.
Go reads this file in utils.TestReleaseLinkCorpus; TypeScript reads the same
file in frontend/lib/releaseLinks.test.ts. Both assert their own half plus the
platform table itself, so a platform, a host, or a rule added to one language
and not the other fails the other language's suite and names the value. A rule
the corpus carries no case for is a rule it cannot police, so add cases with
rules.
platforms   = the whole registry. Each side asserts its own table equals this,
which is what stops the two lists drifting.
maxUrlLength= the shared cap. Here rather than as a literal in each language,
for the same reason the platform table is. Only the NUMBER is
shared: Go counts bytes, TypeScript counts UTF-16 code units.
renderable  = both gates accept.
refused     = the Go write gate refuses. `alsoRefusedByReader` marks the ones
the reader must ALSO refuse, i.e. every case where a click would
leave the platform. The rest are cases where the WRITER is
deliberately the stricter side and a legacy row of that shape
still opens the right page: surrounding whitespace, which the
browser strips, and host spellings the browser's UTS-46 mapping
folds back onto the platform. Refusing those on the read side
would take away links that work.

refused.why: platform is not in the registry, so nothing knows how to anchor it
untrimmed platform: stored verbatim, and the label lookup would miss it
foreign host carrying the platform name in the query; a substring check would pass it
lookalike suffix: the platform name is a LABEL, not the registrable domain
the leading dot in the suffix anchor rejects a domain that merely ends with the base
userinfo spoof: the text before @ is not the host, and both parsers agree it is evil.test
raw link-local IP; the anchor is on the host, never on the URL text
scheme is neither http nor https
scheme is neither http nor https

trailing whitespace: refused at write time so the column never holds a value the two parsers disagree about, but the browser strips it, so a legacy row of this shape opens the right page and the reader still renders it
leading whitespace, same reason
an Apple-owned host, but one that publishes writing by strangers; the anchor names the music host so an Apple Music label cannot head a forum post
same shape on Spotify's forum
same shape on Amazon's retail domain
fully-qualified trailing dot: neither parser normalizes it away, so it does not match the anchor
IPv6 literal is not a platform host
anchors are per platform, not per family: youtu.be is allowlisted for youtube only
backslash: Go's parser refuses it in a host and the browser's ends the authority at it, so both land on evil.test
port above the WHATWG ceiling: the browser's parser throws, so the row could never render. Go takes any run of digits, which is the one divergence where Go is the lenient parser
same ceiling, five digits
malformed punycode label: Go sees four ordinary bytes, the browser's parser decodes it, fails, and throws, so the row could never render

well-formed punycode label. No platform host in the registry is an IDN, so the writer refuses the whole spelling rather than deciding which decode; the reader still renders it, because a legacy row of this shape does open the right page
circled letter: UTS-46 maps it to o, so the browser resolves this onto a bandcamp.com subdomain and renders it
ideographic full stop: UTS-46 makes it a label separator, so the browser resolves this to a bandcamp.com SUBDOMAIN
soft hyphen: UTS-46 deletes it, leaving a bandcamp.com subdomain
non-ASCII label: the browser punycodes it and it stays a bandcamp.com subdomain
backslash before the @: Go's parser refuses it outright, the browser ends the authority at it and lands on bandcamp.com
